{{nihongo|'''Kattamine Shrine'''|刈田嶺神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Mutsu Province]].

[[ja:刈田嶺神社 (刈田岳)]]

'''Kattamine Shrine''' (かったみねじんじゃ) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|abstract|Q845945|ar|جينجا|arz|ضريح شنتو|bcl|Shinto shrine|ca|Jinja|cs|Šintoistická svatyně|da|Shinto-tempel|de|Shintō-Schrein|el|Σιντοϊστικό Ιερό|eo|Ŝintoa sanktejo|es|Jinja|eu|Jinja|fa|معبد شینتویی|fi|Šintolainen pyhäkkö|fr|Sanctuaire shinto|hi|शिंतो मंदिर|hr|Šintoistički hram|hu|Sintó szentély|id|Jinja|it|Jinja|ja|神社|ka|ძინძია|ko|신사 (신토)|lb|Shintō-Schräin|mr|शिंतो मंदिर|nl|Jinja (heiligdom)|no|Jinja|or|ଜିଞ୍ଜା|pl|Jinja|pt|Templo xintoísta|ru|Дзиндзя|sc|Jinja|simple|Shinto shrine|sl|Šintoistično svetišče|sr|Шинтоистички храм|sv|Jinja|th|ศาลเจ้าชินโต|tok|tomo sewi pi nasin sewi Sinto|tr|Şinto tapınağı|uk|Святилище (синто)|uz|Dzindzya|vi|Thần xã|wuu|神社|zh|神社|zh_yue|神社|qid=Q845945}} located on the summit of Mt. Katta ({{ill|Elevation|Q2633778|qid=Q2633778}} 1,758 {{ill|Metre|Q11573|qid=Q11573|lt=m}}), on the {{ill|Miyagi Prefecture|Q47896|qid=Q47896}} side of the {{ill|Mount Zaō|Q167951|qid=Q167951}} in the {{ill|Ōu Mountains|Q1357388|qid=Q1357388}}. It forms a pair with {{ill|Kattamine Shrine|Q11396255|qid=Q11396255|lt=Kattamine Shrine}} located in {{ill|Togatta Onsen|ja|遠刈田温泉|qid=Q11641981}} at the foot of the mountain. This shrine is called the “'''Okumiya''' (Inner Shrine),” while the shrine of the same name in Togatta Onsen is called the “Satomiya (Village Shrine).” The {{ill|Shintai|de|Shintai|el|Σίνταϊ|es|Shintai|fa|شین‌تای|fi|Shintai|fr|Shintai|hr|Shintai|id|Shintai|ja|神体|jv|Shintai|ko|신체 (신토)|mk|Шинтаи|pl|Go-shintai|pt|Shintai|ru|Синтай (синтоизм)|simple|Shintai|sr|Шинтаи|tr|Shintai|uk|Сінтай (синто)|zh|神體|qid=Q327532}} (sacred object) is seasonally {{ill|Shintai|de|Shintai|el|Σίνταϊ|es|Shintai|fa|شین‌تای|fi|Shintai|fr|Shintai|hr|Shintai|id|Shintai|ja|神体|jv|Shintai|ko|신체 (신토)|mk|Шинтаи|pl|Go-shintai|pt|Shintai|ru|Синтай (синтоизм)|simple|Shintai|sr|Шинтаи|tr|Shintai|uk|Сінтай (синто)|zh|神體|qid=Q327532|lt=enshrined}} between the two shrines—at the summit Okumiya in summer and at the Satomiya at the foot of the mountain in winter. The name “Zao Mountains” derives from the {{ill|Zaō Gongen|Q10514059|qid=Q10514059}} that were once worshipped at both shrines.

=== Location ===

It is said that the shrine was originally built atop a boundary mound between Ōshū and Ushū on Mt. Kumano, but because it was close to the crater and frequently burned due to eruptions, it was relocated around the {{ill|Shōhō|Q1146192|qid=Q1146192}} era (1645–1648) to the Omuro (Komedō) area of Mt. Katta after consultation between the Sendai Domain lord and the Matsudaira clan of Yamagata <ref name="ZaoTownHistory1987">Zao Town History Compilation Committee, “Materials on Zao Mountain Worship,” *Zao Town History: Source Materials I*, 1987</ref>.

Since ancient times, three shrines—Zao, {{ill|Hakusan Shrine|Q11579587|qid=Q11579587|lt=Hakusan}}, and {{ill|Kumano shrine|Q3200355|qid=Q3200355|lt=Kumano}}—were enshrined on Mt. Kumano (elevation 1,841 m), the highest peak in the Zao range, and their village shrines still exist on both the Ōshū and Ushū sides. Along the main pilgrimage route (Miyagi side), the {{ill|Torii|Q234731|qid=Q234731}} gates were erected as follows: the third torii at the Ōtorii enclosure in Maruta, Zao Town; the second torii at Iboishi; and the first torii at Fudō Falls. According to the documents of Sanjō-in at the Hōzawa route, the ritual method of worshipping the three shrines represents the correct ancient mountain practice <ref name="ZaoTownHistory1987" />.

In {{ill|1907|Q2048|qid=Q2048}} ({{ill|Meiji era|Q3125096|qid=Q3125096}} 40), in the document “Shrine Survey Report” submitted by Kattamine Shrine (classified as a village shrine) included in *Survey of Shrines and Temples: Sendai City, Katta District, Shibata District, Volume 1 of 9* (held by the Miyagi Prefectural Archives), the shrine’s location is recorded as “enshrined at Kuraishi-dake, Miyamura, Katta District.” The report is dated July 4, Meiji 39, and lists Shrine Administrator Fujimoto Kunio and parish representatives from Miyamura, Katta District (present-day {{ill|Zaō, Miyagi|Q1347874|qid=Q1347874}}), with some residing in Sendai City.

On the other hand, the {{ill|Zaō, Miyagi|Q1347874|qid=Q1347874}} Board of Education states that the shrine is located in {{ill|Shichikashuku, Miyagi|Q1204398|qid=Q1204398}}, Katta District <ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dokitan.com/column/02.html|title=Dokitan.com > History Column > No. 2 Kattamine Shrine (1)|publisher=Zao Town Board of Education|date=2009-05-03|accessdate=2025-07-06}}</ref>.

=== History ===
The shrine is identified as “Kattamine Shrine (Myōjin Taisha)” in the Katta District entry of the *{{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932}}* (*Engishiki*, Volumes 9–10, {{ill|Enchō|de|Enchō|fa|انچو|fr|Ère Enchō|ia|Encho|id|Enchō|ja|延長 (元号)|ko|엔초|ru|Энтё|simple|Enchō|sr|Енчо|tr|Enchō|uk|Ентьо|zh|延長 (日本)|zh_yue|延長 (年號)|qid=Q1327274}} 5 [927]).

The *{{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|cs|Nihon Sandai Džicuroku|de|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|es|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|fa|نیهون ساندای جیتسوروکو|ff|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|fr|Nihon sandai jitsuroku|it|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|ja|日本三代実録|ko|일본삼대실록|pt|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|ru|Нихон сандай дзицуроку|simple|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|zh|日本三代實錄|zh_classical|日本三代實錄|qid=Q1052981}}* records its establishment in {{ill|Engi (era)|Q1374325|qid=Q1374325}} 1 (901). In {{ill|Jōgan|Q1075635|qid=Q1075635|lt=Jōgan}} 11 (869), the year of the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Jōgan tsunami}} , the deity “Kattamine-no-Kami,” ranked Junior Ninth Rank, was promoted by extraordinary advancement to Junior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade. {{ill|Sakuma Dōgan|Q6562843|qid=Q6562843}} remarked “How sudden indeed,” suggesting that some records may be missing. {{ill|Tōgo Yoshida|Q11413910|qid=Q11413910}} interpreted the Jōgan tsunami as a “divine calamity caused by volcanic awe,” viewing it as the “wrath of the mountain god” as understood by the imperial court. In contrast, the “Shrine Survey Report” cited above quotes from the *{{ill|Ruijū Kokushi|Q1038639|qid=Q1038639}}* (compiled {{ill|Kanpyō (era)|Q1346292|qid=Q1346292}} 4 [892]), a rearrangement of the {{ill|Rikkokushi|Q1151168|qid=Q1151168}}, stating that the rank promotion was due to considerations of harvest conditions and drought or flood, without mentioning the tsunami.

According to *Kinpu Sanzan Goengi*, the Zao Daigongen enshrined on Mt. Zao (Mt. Fubo) was opened by {{ill|En no Gyōja|Q198946|qid=Q198946}} in {{ill|Hakuhō|Q11580612|qid=Q11580612}} 8 (679). It is also said to have been invited by his uncle Gangyō. The Zao Daigongen Shrine long supervised the ascetics of the Zao region, managed by Gankyō-ji Temple at the eastern foot of Ōkattayama (Aomayama). *Kinpusan Kai-en narabi ni Higashidake Onsen Raireki* records that it was later revived by the monk Jitsugan, a spiritual descendant of {{ill|Kūkai|Q222227|qid=Q222227|lt=Kōbō Daishi}}.

By the late {{ill|Heian period|Q193292|qid=Q193292}} (late {{ill|12th century|Q7061|qid=Q7061}}), the shrine prospered under the patronage of the {{ill|Northern Fujiwara|ar|فوجيوارا الشمالية|cs|Severní Fudžiwarové|fa|خاندان فوجیوارای شمالی|ff|Northern Fujiwara|fr|Ōshū Fujiwara|ja|奥州藤原氏|ko|오슈 후지와라씨|pt|Clã Ōshū Fujiwara|ru|Северные Фудзивара|uk|Муцівські Фудзівара|zh|奧州藤原氏|qid=Q1050942}}, with Gankyō-ji expanding to 48 sub-temples. After the clan’s fall, decline and destruction by warfare led to ruin, and following the {{ill|Ōnin War|Q385676|qid=Q385676}}, only three temples remained: Sannobō, Miyamotobō, and Takenobō <ref name="Fūdo-ki">Tanabe Marefumi, *Fūnai Fudoki*, 1772</ref>.

Sannobō later fell into ruin around the {{ill|Enpō|Q1145735|qid=Q1145735}} era. Miyamotobō became Kyūrenzō-ji during the {{ill|Tenshō (Momoyama period)|Q1145058|qid=Q1145058}} era (1573–1592), when Lord {{ill|Date Masamune|ban|Date Masamune|ca|Date Masamune|cs|Masamune Date|da|Date Masamune|de|Date Masamune|es|Date Masamune|fa|داته ماسامونه|fi|Date Masamune|fr|Date Masamune|hu|Date Maszamune|id|Date Masamune|it|Date Masamune|ja|伊達政宗|ko|다테 마사무네|la|Idates Massamunes|ms|Date Masamune|nl|Date Masamune|no|Date Masamune|pl|Masamune Date|pms|Date Masamune|pt|Date Masamune|ro|Masamune Date|ru|Датэ Масамунэ|simple|Date Masamune|sk|Masamune Date|sr|Масамуне Дате|sv|Date Masamune|th|ดาเตะ มาซามูเนะ|tr|Date Masamune|uk|Дате Масамуне|vi|Date Masamune|zh|伊達政宗|zh_classical|伊達政宗|zh_min_nan|Date Masamune|zh_yue|伊達政宗|qid=Q311183}} granted it the mountain and temple name “Hōchizan Renzō-ji” and donated 200 koku of land. By longstanding precedent, Renzō-ji assumed administrative control over the shrine. Takenobō, known as Kinpusan Zao-ji Takenobō, oversaw the main pilgrimage route. During the {{ill|Ōan|Q1146245|qid=Q1146245}} era of the {{ill|Northern Court|Q1201819|qid=Q1201819}} (1368–1374), three Tendai ascetic offices—Sanjō-in, Anraku-in, and Kakuzembō—were established at different approaches, collectively called the Ushū Three Bettō, all operating under Takenobō’s direction. In the late {{ill|Edo period|Q184963|qid=Q184963}}, as mountain pilgrimage flourished, they guided many worshippers to the summit shrine, though this prosperity later led to disputes over rights, culminating in lawsuits during the {{ill|Kaei|Q1146125|qid=Q1146125}} era (1848–1855).

The 1907 *Shrine Survey* notes that the place name “Kattadake” was of relatively modern origin, with the mountain historically called Fubōsan or Zaodake, also known as Kuraishidake. It explains that because the shrine was enshrined on the summit of Ōkattayama, the divine name “Kattamine Shrine” was adopted, though confusion over the name remains.

With the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|Q8707|qid=Q8707}} and enforcement of the Shinto–Buddhist separation edicts, “Zao Gongen” was adopted as a Shinto divine name in Yoshino, and monks became Shinto priests. Following this, in July {{ill|1869|Q7720|qid=Q7720}}, the name was changed from “Zao Daigongen” to “Zao Ōkami,” and the shrine was called “Zao Shrine.” In September the same year, based on the interpretation that “Zao Ōkami” referred to the two deities {{ill|Mikumari|Q11129547|qid=Q11129547|lt=Ame-no-Mikumari-no-Kami and Kuni-no-Mikumari-no-Kami}}, the shrine was renamed “Mikumari Shrine.” By 1875, it came to be called “Kattamine Shrine.”

=== Seasonal Relocation ===
A map of the Togatta residence created by the Katakura family around the {{ill|Kanbun (era)|Q1146228|qid=Q1146228}} era does not show a “Zao Daigongen Temporary Shrine,” instead marking “Takenobō” at the current Satomiya location.

*Ōu Kanshiki Monrōshi* (1719) records that a shrine of Zao Gongen stood on the summit, with torii gates along the eastern mountain paths. April 8 was called the “Opening,” when snow melted and roads opened, while October 8 marked the “Closing.” During winter, villagers held rites with steamed rice and cloudy sake.

*An’ei Fudoki Goyōshodashi* (1777) records a “Zao Gongen Temporary Shrine,” noting that due to heavy snow, the deity was relocated downhill on October 8 and returned on April 8. The temporary shrine stood at the same location as Takenobō, indicating a close relationship.

Today, relocation between the Satomiya and Okumiya coincides with the opening of the Zao Echo Line and {{ill|Zao High Line|Q11621931|qid=Q11621931}} roads, typically in late April, though timing varies by snowfall. Before relocation, {{ill|Ōsaki Hachimangū|Q874428|qid=Q874428}} in {{ill|Sendai|Q46747|qid=Q46747}} performs annual snow-clearing service to expose the shrine buildings and approach paths.

=== Access ===
[[File:Kattamine shrine winter.jpg|thumb|The shrine during severe winter when roads are closed<br />(Photo taken March 9, 2006)]]
{{seealso|Okama (Zao Mountains)}}
From the free Zao Echo Line, enter the Zao Highline (daytime toll road), park at the free Katta Pass parking lot in front of the Miyagi Prefectural Zao Rest House, then walk about 15 minutes.

For winter closures, see {{ill|Miyagi Prefectural Road and Yamagata Prefectural Road Route 12|Q11453957|qid=Q11453957}}.
